AI-DRIVEN HERBAL SKINCARE FORMULATION OPTIMIZATION AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名: AI本草護膚配方最佳化極限 AI-Driven Herbal Skincare Formulation Optimization at the Limit is a 777-page English prospective research monograph on whether artificial intelligence can make genuinely better, externally reconstructable herbal skincare formulation predictions for previously unseen raw-material lots. Its core three-coupling is AI modeling, formulation constraints, and external generalization. The central falsifiable test is not a favorable random-split score: a model frozen in advance must survive complete raw-material-lot holdouts and forward-in-time evaluation against strong, resource-matched conventional baselines. The study separates botanical species and chemotype authentication, formula mass-fraction closure, sample and instrument provenance, physicochemical endpoints, safety restrictions and predictive uncertainty. It tests whether nominal AI improvements are explained instead by duplicate aliquots, batch identifiers, chronological leakage, correlated chemistry, imbalance across rare botanical families or extra measurement budget. It preserves original outcome units and treats unsafe or unqualified ingredient combinations as hard exclusions rather than soft optimization penalties. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates cover external risk, compositional closure and log ratios, hierarchical lot variance, analytical censoring, physical rheology and diffusion, Gaussian-process predictions, constrained acquisition, Pareto comparisons, distribution shift, calibrated intervals, noncompensatory safety gates and evidence provenance. Eighty-two research chapters are followed by 410 individually paginated studies. Two hundred Research Gates pose prospective falsification questions, including blinded material substitution, negative controls, independent metrology, worst-supplier performance, safe abstention and external replay. Thirty-three different Phoenix Answer Embryos propose distinct testable instruments, protocols, audits and evidence artifacts for future investigators. This manuscript is a hypothesis-forming, nonclinical Research Working Edition. It does not report an executed integrated experiment, verified cosmetic benefit, human safety trial, regulatory approval, or a qualified production system. The three STARLI mother works provide methodological ancestry rather than direct evidence that this skincare optimization works. External DOI sources are identified by their bounded roles in formulation science, machine-learning evaluation, scientific-data stewardship and evidence reporting.
